summary: Specifies the "tel" URI scheme, which identifies resources by telephone number. It makes a phone number usable as a link. It obsoletes RFC 2806.

eli5.summary: It is a way to write a phone number as a link, so clicking it can start a call.

questions: how to write a phone number as a uri
what is phone-context in a tel uri
tel uri global vs local number
how to add an extension to a tel uri
subtitle: How to write a telephone number as a URI, global or local, without saying how to dial it.

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers need a standard URI form so they can appear in web pages, address books and protocols such as SIP, without mixing up the number itself with the keys a user presses to dial it.
tldr.mechanism: The tel: scheme carries a telephone number as an identifier, either global (starting with +) or local with a mandatory phone-context parameter, plus optional parameters such as extension and ISDN subaddress.
tldr.outcome: Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2806 and is updated by RFC 5341. A tel URI names a number, it does not say how to reach it.

today: RFC 3966 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2806 and is updated by RFC 5341.

sections.title: Numbers as Identifiers, Not Dial Strings
sections.content:
The tel URI describes resources identified by telephone numbers. A telephone number here is a string of decimal digits that uniquely indicates a network termination point, public or private, fixed or wireless. The terminal can support any electronic communication service, including voice, data and fax.

The RFC separates two ideas. An address-of-record (identifier) is the canonical number for a termination point. A dial string is what a user actually enters, which may include digits to exit a PBX or post-dial DTMF tones. The tel URI covers only the first. It is a globally unique name and does not describe the steps needed to reach the number or imply dialling semantics.

The consequence is that services such as electronic banking or voicemail cannot be specified in a tel URI. The URI also does not name the call type, such as voice, fax or data; that is negotiated in-band or by a signaling protocol such as SIP.
sections.eli5: A tel link is like a name tag with a phone number on it. It says whose number it is, but it does not tell your phone which buttons to press.

sections.title: URI Syntax
sections.content:
A tel URI is tel: followed by a global number or a local number. The syntax is given in ABNF. A global number is a + followed by digits, optionally with visual separators (hyphen, full stop and round brackets). Parameters follow after semicolons, such as ;ext=, ;isub= and ;phone-context=.

The reserved characters +, ;, = and ? MUST NOT be percent encoded when used as delimiters, but MUST be percent encoded inside parameter values. No parameter name, the ISDN subaddress, the extension or the context may appear more than once.

Order is fixed: the isub or ext parameter comes first if present, then phone-context, then any other parameters in lexicographical order. This makes character-by-character comparison simpler, for example in SIP URIs.
sections.eli5: The link always starts with 'tel:' and then the number. Extra details like an extension go after semicolons, always in the same order.

sections.title: Comparing tel URIs
sections.content:
Two tel URIs are equivalent when both are local or both are global (start with +), their digits are equal after removing all visual separators, and their parameters match. A phone-context is compared as a host name if it is a domain name, or digit by digit (after removing separators) if it is a global number.

Parameters are matched by name regardless of order. If one URI has a parameter name the other lacks, the two are not equal. Comparison is case-insensitive, yet all parameter names and values SHOULD use lower case because tel URIs may be used where comparison is case sensitive.
sections.eli5: Dashes and dots are just decoration. If two links have the same digits and the same extras, they point to the same phone.

sections.title: Global and Local Numbers
sections.content:
All phone numbers MUST use the global form unless they cannot be represented that way. A global number is marked by the leading +, is composed of a country code and a national number as in E.123 and E.164, is unambiguous everywhere and SHOULD be used. Numbers from private numbering plans, emergency numbers such as "911" and "112", and service codes such as "411" cannot be global and must be local numbers. Implementations MUST NOT assume numbers have a maximum, minimum or fixed length.

A local number is unique only within some area or part of the network, such as a PBX or a country. It MUST carry a phone-context parameter naming the scope in which it is unique, so that context plus number is globally unique again. Local numbers SHOULD NOT be used unless there is no global form, because both sides must be configured to insert and recognize the right context.

The context is either the leading digits of a global number or a domain name. For example, +49-6151-16 would be a suitable context for an organization that owns all numbers starting with those digits, and houston.example.com is a domain-name context. The domain does not have to resolve to a host but must be under the control of the entity managing the context. A context made of global digits does not mean that prepending them yields a valid E.164 number: "911" is labelled with the context +1, but +1-911 is not a valid E.164 number.

Alphabetic keypad letters, as in 1-555-IETF-RFC, are not supported in the URI, because the letter-to-digit mapping is not uniform internationally.
sections.eli5: A global number is like a full address with the country on it. A local number is like 'room 7042', which only makes sense once you say which building, and that is the context.

sections.title: Extensions, Subaddresses and Other Parameters
sections.content:
The isub parameter carries an ISDN subaddress. Subaddresses typically hold International Alphabet 5 characters but may contain any octet value. The ext parameter identifies a station behind a non-ISDN PBX and is roughly equivalent to an ISDN subaddress. At most one of the two can appear in a tel URI.

Future extensions may add parameters, either mandatory or optional. Mandatory parameters start with m-. An implementation MAY ignore optional parameters but MUST NOT use a URI with an unknown mandatory parameter. In this document phone-context is mandatory, while isub and ext are optional. New mandatory parameters need a standards-track RFC, and an informational RFC is enough for optional ones. Forwarding entities MUST NOT delete or modify optional parameters they do not understand.
sections.eli5: Extra details, like an extension number, ride along as labelled notes. If a program does not know a note that is marked essential, it must not use the link.

sections.title: Use in HTML and with SIP
sections.content:
In HTML, a link SHOULD enclose the telephone number itself, rather than text such as "this number", so users can predict the action. On a public page the number in the URI SHOULD always be in global form, even if the visible text uses a local format.

SIP can use a tel URI anywhere a URI is allowed, for example as a Request-URI. Unless the user agent connects straight to a PSTN gateway, a proxy, typically the outbound proxy, has to translate the tel URI to a SIP URI pointing at a gateway. A proxy MUST NOT translate local-number URIs whose contexts it does not understand. If a proxy cannot find a route for the context, it returns a 404 (Not Found) response.

Translating what a user dials into a tel or SIP URI is the job of a dial plan in the end system. To avoid ambiguity, the dial plan MUST insert a suitable phone-context when it translates. Section 7 of the RFC also explains why tel is a separate scheme: it describes reaching a number independently of how, be it a SIP-to-PSTN gateway, ENUM, H.323 or a circuit-switched call.
sections.eli5: On a web page, the link text should show the real number so you know what you are about to call. Inside phone networks, a helper server turns the tel link into a route to a gateway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations parallel those of the mailto URL. Web clients and similar tools MUST NOT use a tel URI to place calls without the explicit consent of the user. The RFC lists the risks: calls may cost money, the URI may place malicious or annoying calls, a call takes the phone line off-hook, and a call may reveal an unlisted number in caller identification data and let an attacker link it to other information such as an e-mail or IP address.

HTML links make this worse, since the link text can hide the true target, for example a link reading "Find free information here" that points at a 900 number. Finally, tel URIs can leak private information like phone numbers in text do, and the tel: prefix may make such numbers easier for an adversary to find with a search engine.
sections.eli5: A link that starts a phone call without asking could cost you money or give away your number. So the program must always ask first.

items.title: Abuse
items.text: The URI may be used to place malicious or annoying calls.

items.title: Line in use
items.text: A call takes the phone line off-hook, preventing its use.

items.title: Exposure
items.text: Caller identification may reveal an unlisted number and let it be correlated with other information.
